passage:
[1] Anyone who has walked past the library in Brennock Park knows the granite fountain beside its steps, even if they have never seen it run. Its bronze spout has been dry for decades, and its basin hoards leaves and paper cups. Eleven fountains like it stand across our town, all of them capped. We believe the town council should restore every one, and we believe the cost is smaller than it looks.

[2] Public fountains were once a point of civic pride. In the late 1800s, towns across the country installed them, many paid for by temperance societies that hoped free, clean water would keep thirsty workers out of the saloons. Ours were built in that spirit. For most of a century, the fountains upkeep was a routine line in the parks budget. Then, as the pipes aged and repairs grew expensive, the council capped them one at a time.

[3] What replaced them is the vending machine. A bottle of water at the park kiosk now costs more than a gallon from the tap costs at home, and the empty bottles, which pile up in every bin by evening, have to be hauled away at public expense. Every fountain we restore means less plastic bottles in those bins. Residents who cannot spare the money simply go without. On hot afternoons we have watched people cup water from the splash pad in their hands. Those people are not careless, they have nowhere else to drink.

[4] Dale Ferris, a plumber the council consulted last spring, estimated that reviving each fountain with a filter and a lead-free spout would cost about four thousand dollars. For all eleven, that comes to roughly forty-four thousand dollars, paid once. For example, the money would have to come from somewhere, most likely the fund set aside for resurfacing the tennis courts. The tennis courts can chill for a year.

[5] The council takes up the parks budget on the second Tuesday of next month. We urge every reader to attend and to ask for the fountains by name. Other towns have done this, and so can we.
prompt: Which choice most effectively concludes the essay by returning to the scene with which it opens, in place of "Other towns have done this, and so can we."?
choices: No Change
Then the granite fountain beside the library steps can finally run again.
Then the people at the splash pad will not have to drink from their hands.
Then the temperance societies' old promise of free water will be kept.
correct_answer: Then the granite fountain beside the library steps can finally run again.
explanation: The essay opens on one image: the dry granite fountain beside the library steps that no one has seen run. Ending with that fountain running again brings the reader back to it and shows the editorial's request granted. The original sentence makes a general appeal and refers to no scene at all. The people at the splash pad come from paragraph 3, and the temperance societies come from paragraph 2; each ending is true to the essay but returns to a later paragraph rather than to the opening one.

passage:
[1] A tardigrade is easy to overlook. Most species measure less than a millimeter, and each of them spend its life clambering on eight stubby legs through the thin film of water that coats a clump of moss. That film is a precarious home. On a sunny afternoon it can evaporate within an hour. Leaving the animal with no water at all. Without water, the proteins inside a cell lose their folded shapes and the cell's membranes tear. As a result, drying out kills nearly every other animal. A tardigrade simply waits.

[2] [A] As the moss dries, the tardigrade draws in its head and legs and contracts into a compact, barrel-shaped form that biologists call a tun. [B] Inside the tun, the animal gives up nearly all of its water. [C] Its metabolism slows until it can scarcely be measured, and it stays that way for as long as the drought lasts. [D]

[3] Biologists have identified two main defenses: a sugar and a set of unusual proteins. Trehalose, which some species build up in their cells as they dry takes the place of water around delicate molecules. The proteins are stranger still, because they occur in no other animal. As the cell dries, the proteins that each tardigrade produces forms a glass-like solid, and like amber around an insect, the solid holds everything in place until water returns.

[4] The tun is also remarkably durable. Tardigrades in that state have endured conditions that would destroy most other living things. Dried and sealed away, researchers have revived tardigrades after several years in storage.

[5] When water comes back, the process runs in reverse. The tun soaks up moisture, the glass-like solid dissolves, and the animal had stretched out its legs. Within an hour or so it swells back to its normal shape and size again as before and resumes its slow walk through the moss, as though the drought had been only a pause.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "The tun soaks up moisture, the glass-like solid dissolves, and the animal had stretched out its legs," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "had stretched"?
choices: No Change
stretches
stretched
will have stretched
explanation: The sentence lists three steps of one process in the present tense ("soaks," "dissolves"), and the essay explains what tardigrades generally do, so the third verb must also be present: "stretches." "Had stretched" places the action before the other two, as if the animal stretched before it had absorbed any water; "stretched" breaks the present-tense series; and "will have stretched" projects the step into the future.

passage_title: The Day the Railroads Set the Clocks
passage:
[1] Until the 1880s, most American towns kept their own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the town, so noon in one city arrived a few minutes earlier or later than noon in the next. For people who rarely traveled far from home, the differences hardly mattered.

[2] The railroads changed that. A passenger heading west from Boston passed through dozens of local times, and each railroad company kept its own time as well, usually that of the city where it had its headquarters. A large station might display several clocks, each showing a different hour for a different line. Boston's clocks, set each day by a signal from a nearby observatory, were among the most accurate in the country. Timetables became puzzles that required arithmetic, worse, schedules that disagreed by even a few minutes made collisions on single-track lines more likely.

[3] Railroad managers, who had argued about reform for years, finally acted in 1883. The plan they adopted divided the country into four time zones. Each zone was roughly fifteen degrees of longitude wide. Within a zone, every railroad clock would show the same time. On November 18, 1883 railroad clocks across the country were reset at noon. Operators sent out telegraph signals simultaneously at the very same instant, and station clocks were adjusted to match. In cities east of a zone's center, clocks were turned back several minutes, so residents heard the noon bells ring twice.

[4] Not everyone welcomed the change. Some newspapers complained that the railroads had done something no government had ever dared, they had rearranged the sun. A few cities kept their local time for years. Similarly, the convenience of a single shared hour won out, and holdout towns set their clocks by the railroad. In 1918, Congress made the zones law.

[5] Today the arrangement seems as natural as the weather. Few people who check the time on a phone know that the lines dividing one hour from the next were drawn first on railroad maps.
prompt: In paragraph 4, which choice provides the most logical transition in place of "Similarly," in the sentence that begins "Similarly, the convenience of a single shared hour won out"?
choices: No Change
Eventually,
For instance,
Thus,
explanation: The previous sentence says a few cities kept their local time "for years"; this sentence tells what happened after those years, when the holdouts finally gave in. That is a later point in time, which "Eventually" marks. "Similarly" would present the adoption as like the resistance, though it is the end of it; "For instance" would offer it as an example of cities keeping local time; and "Thus" would make the resistance the cause of its own defeat.

passage:
[1] Most mornings in January, Wren Halvorsen is on a ridge above the ski area before the lifts begin to turn. Beside her, Tamsin a border collie with one white ear, watches the slope. Halvorsen works on the ski patrol, and Tamsin is trained to find people buried under avalanche wreckage. Teaching her to do it has taken four winters.

[2] Border collies were first bred to herd sheep in the hill country along the border between England and Scotland. At first, a volunteer runs a few yards away, waving a tug toy, and ducks behind a snowbank while the dog watches. Later the volunteer hides out of sight, and the dog has to follow her nose instead of her eyes. In the final stage, a volunteer waits in a cave dug into the slope and sealed with blocks of snow. Hidden inside the cave, the dog can find the volunteer only by his scent.

[3] Scent is the whole point. A buried person gives off an odor that rises through the snow, and a dog can search a slope far faster than a line of patrollers pushing probe poles into it. That speed matters, because the odds of surviving a burial fall steeply once the first fifteen minutes have passed. Wind and weather complicate the search. In contrast, a crosswind can carry the odor many yards downslope, so Tamsin may first show interest well below the spot where the person actually lies.

[4] [A] When Tamsin reaches the strongest scent, she digs and barks at the spot. [B] Halvorsen pushes a probe into the snow to confirm the find, and the other patrollers start shoveling. [C] Tamsin's reward comes only after the volunteer is uncovered: a few minutes of tug-of-war with the same toy she chased in her first games of hide-and-seek. [D]

[5] On a real search there is no toy waiting, Halvorsen carries one in her pocket anyway. Another patroller, who began training a dog of her own last winter, now asks Halvorsen for advice, and on slow afternoons Halvorsen hides in snow caves so that the patrollers dog can practice finding a stranger. Every hour a young dog spends digging her out of a cave, she says, is an hour it will not have to spend learning on a real slide.
prompt: In paragraph 2, in the sentence "Hidden inside the cave, the dog can find the volunteer only by his scent," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "the dog can find the volunteer only by his scent"?
choices: No Change
the volunteer can be located only by his scent
only his scent can lead the dog to the volunteer
the dog's only guide to the volunteer is his scent
correct_answer: the volunteer can be located only by his scent
explanation: The opening phrase "Hidden inside the cave" describes the volunteer, so a dangling-modifier rule applies: the noun it modifies must be the subject that follows the comma. Only "the volunteer can be located only by his scent" puts "the volunteer" there. The original makes the dog the one hidden in the cave. "Only his scent can lead the dog" makes the scent the thing hidden, and "the dog's only guide" makes the subject "guide," so the phrase still attaches to the wrong noun.

passage:
[1] For nine years I waited for the 7:14 train with my earbuds in, reading the morning's email before I had even reached my desk. The platform at Kellerton station backs onto a strip of scrub and young maples, and I must have stood beside it two thousand times without once wondering what was making all that noise.

[2] That changed on the morning my phone died. With nothing to look at. I watched a woman at the far end of the platform who stood perfectly still, her head tilted toward the trees. When I finally asked what she was doing, she said she was counting. Her name was Corinne. She had ridden the 7:14 for longer than I had, and she could name every bird singing in that strip of trees without seeing one of them.

[3] I asked her for a lesson, and she gave me only a rule. Songs, she said, have to be learned one at a time and by ear, the way you come to know a friend's voice on the phone. Of all the birds in the strip, the cardinal was the easier to learn, since its song sounds like someone whistling for a dog. The song sparrow—a plain brown bird I had never once noticed, begins with a few clear notes and then dissolves into a buzzy trill.

[4] Even those two took longer than I had expected. For the first month, every bird sounded like every other bird. Then, one gray morning in April, a sparrow sings, and I knew it was a sparrow before I had turned my head. I walked to the office that morning feeling like an absolute legend.

[5] Still, I would not call myself a birder. The notebook holds eleven names, and the two thrushes songs still sound identical to me. I read my email on the train now instead of on the platform, and the first ten minutes of each morning belong to whoever happens to be singing.
prompt: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the last sentence of paragraph 3: "That evening I bought a pocket notebook and wrote both birds on its first page, with the date beside each." Should the writer make this addition here?
choices: Yes, because it introduces the notebook that paragraph 5 later mentions as though the reader already knows about it.
Yes, because it explains how the narrator was able to recognize the sparrow before turning to look at it in April.
No, because it shifts paragraph 3 away from what Corinne taught the narrator and toward the narrator's own habits.
No, because paragraph 4 already makes clear that learning the cardinal and the song sparrow took longer than expected.
correct_answer: Yes, because it introduces the notebook that paragraph 5 later mentions as though the reader already knows about it.
explanation: Paragraph 5 says "The notebook holds eleven names," using "the" as if the notebook were already familiar, yet nothing earlier mentions one; the added sentence supplies it and also starts the count that paragraph 5 reports. Writing down names and dates does not explain recognizing a song by ear, which the essay credits to a month of listening. The shift toward the narrator's habits is real but harmless, since paragraph 3 already ends on the narrator's own experience of the sparrow. That paragraph 4 says learning was slow is true, but it does nothing to account for the notebook.

passage:
[1] A suspension bridge hangs its deck from two main cables, and those cables carry the deck's weight over the towers to anchorages set in rock or concrete on each shore. On a large bridge, each cable may be more than half a meter thick. A cable cannot be made in a factory and lifted into place, because at its full, complete size it would be far too heavy and weighty to hoist. Instead, it is spun in the air where it will hang, one wire at a time.

[2] [A] Their first task is to string a temporary footbridge, called a catwalk, from one anchorage to the other, draping it over the tops of both towers along the path each cable will follow. [B] Above the catwalk runs a haul rope that a motor drives in an endless loop, much like the cable of a ski lift. [C] Grooved spinning wheels are clipped to the rope, and as it turns they ride back and forth between the anchorages. [D]

[3] Each spinning wheel carries a loop of wire pulled from a reel at one anchorage. When the wheel reaches the far anchorage, a worker lifts it off and slips it around a steel fitting called a strand shoe. The wheel then heads back for another loop. Because a loop has two sides, every crossing lays down two wires, each only about five millimeters thick. Workers along the catwalk watch each crossing, measure the sag of the new wire, and are adjusting it by hand when it hangs too low or too high.

[4] The wires are gathered into strands of a few hundred each, dozens of strands make up a single cable. When the last strand has been laid and adjusted, a hydraulic machine squeezes the bundle into a dense, round cylinder. Workers then wrap the cylinder in a tight spiral of soft wire and paint it to keep out water.

[5] Suspension bridges include some of the longest spans in the world. Building a cable this way is slow, however, it spares builders from lifting a cable that no crane could raise. Instead, the finished cable does not depend on any single wire. A flaw in one of them affects only a tiny share of the load, and the thousands of others carry on as before.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "Building a cable this way is slow, however, it spares builders from lifting a cable that no crane could raise," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "slow, however, it"?
choices: No Change
slow; however, it
slow however it
slow, however; it
explanation: "Building a cable this way is slow" and "it spares builders from lifting a cable that no crane could raise" are both independent clauses, and "however" is a conjunctive adverb, which cannot join clauses by itself. A semicolon goes before it to separate the clauses and a comma after it: "slow; however, it." The original is a comma splice. Dropping all punctuation fuses the clauses into a run-on. "Slow, however; it" puts the semicolon on the wrong side, attaching "however" to the first clause and leaving the comma to join the clauses.

passage:
[1] When a character in a film walks across a gravel driveway, the crunch the audience hears was almost never recorded on that driveway. Microphones on a set are aimed at the dialogue, they pick up footsteps, rustling coats, and clinking cups only faintly. Those sounds are added afterward, in a studio, by specialists called Foley artists.

[2] The craft takes its name from Jack Foley, a Universal Studios employee who begins adding sounds to films in the late 1920s, when movies first acquired soundtracks. His method, which is still the basis of the work, was simple: watch the picture on a screen and perform the sounds in time with it.

[3] A Foley studio looks less like a recording booth than a cluttered garage. Its floor is divided into shallow pits of sand, gravel, wood, and tile, and the shelves along its back wall holds shoes, gloves, keys, and boxes of objects chosen for how they sound rather than how they look. A bunch of celery, snapped close to the microphone, qualifies as a broken bone. Cornstarch squeezed inside a leather pouch makes the squeak of boots in fresh snow.

[4] What matters most, though, is timing. An artist walking in place on a gravel pit must set each foot down at the instant the actor on screen does and must match the weight and mood of the performance as well. A tired soldier and a nervous thief do not put their feet down the same way. In fact, experienced Foley artists often say that they act with their feet.

[5] Digital libraries now hold millions of recorded sounds. An editor can drop a stock footstep into a scene in seconds. Studios also hire Foley artists. A library footstep is identical every time it plays, whereas a performed one carries the small irregularities of a real persons stride, and audiences hear the difference even when they cannot name it.
prompt: In paragraph 4, the writer is considering deleting the following sentence: "A tired soldier and a nervous thief do not put their feet down the same way." Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
choices: Kept, because it makes the claim about matching weight and mood concrete, and the closing remark about acting with the feet depends on it.
Kept, because it shows that Foley artists choose a different gravel pit for each character depending on how heavy the actor is.
Deleted, because it moves the paragraph away from timing, the subject its first sentence announces, and toward the characters in the film.
Deleted, because it repeats the earlier point that an artist must set each foot down at the instant the actor on screen does.
correct_answer: Kept, because it makes the claim about matching weight and mood concrete, and the closing remark about acting with the feet depends on it.
explanation: The preceding sentence makes an abstract claim, that an artist must match "the weight and mood of the performance," and this sentence turns it into a case a reader can hear: a tired soldier and a nervous thief step differently. The closing remark that Foley artists "act with their feet" depends on that contrast, so it should be kept. Nothing in the paragraph says artists switch gravel pits by character or by the actor's weight, so that reason for keeping it is unsupported. It does not abandon the paragraph's subject: matching weight and mood is part of the timing work the paragraph describes, and the soldier and thief illustrate the artist's job rather than the film's plot. Nor does it repeat the timing point; landing on the same instant and landing in the same manner are different requirements.

passage:
[1] Harbors can be found along nearly every stretch of coast. The hall's wide doors stand open, and its concrete floor, hosed down an hour ago, shines under rows of hanging lamps. The boats that came in overnight have already unloaded. Their catch lies in shallow plastic crates packed in ice: mackerel, squid, a few flat gray skates, and one tuna so large that it has a pallet to itself.

[2] The buyers who arrive earliest, are usually the restaurant owners. In rubber boots and heavy sweaters, they walk the rows slowly, lifting each fish by the gills to look at its eyes. A clear eye means a fish was caught recently; a cloudy one means it has sat on ice too long. Nobody says much, and you find yourself whispering, as if in a library.

[3] Likewise, a bell rings at five o'clock, and the auctioneer climbs onto an upturned crate. He does not call out prices so much as sing them, in a rapid chant that moves quickly and never seems to pause for breath. Standing at the edge of the crowd, the chant sounds like one long, unbroken word. The buyers follow it perfectly. A raised finger counts as a bid, and the auctioneer points at whoever bids first. A buyer who hesitates, even brief, loses the crate to someone else, and a sale can be over in less than ten seconds.

[4] By six o'clock the hall is nearly empty. The tuna goes last. Bought by a man in a gray cap who has not said a word all morning. Forklifts carry the crates out to refrigerated trucks, and by the time you walk back along the seawall, with the sun finally up and the gulls circling the empty boats, the fish you watched being sold are already on their way to kitchens across the city.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "He does not call out prices so much as sing them, in a rapid chant that moves quickly and never seems to pause for breath," which choice is most concise and grammatically acceptable in place of "in a rapid chant that moves quickly and never seems to pause for breath"?
choices: No Change
in a rapid chant that never seems to pause for breath
in a rapid, fast-moving chant that never seems to pause for breath
in a rapid chant, never seems to pause for breath
correct_answer: in a rapid chant that never seems to pause for breath
explanation: A "rapid" chant already moves quickly, so "that moves quickly" repeats it. "In a rapid chant that never seems to pause for breath" keeps the speed and the breathlessness once each. "Rapid, fast-moving" says the same thing twice in a row. Dropping "that" is shorter but leaves "never seems to pause for breath" as a verb with no subject, so the sentence no longer works grammatically.

passage:
[1] Until the middle of the nineteenth century, nobody could tell a ship's captain what the weather would do tomorrow. Sailors read the clouds and their barometers, but a storm moving in from the Atlantic usually arrived faster than any news of it could. The telegraph changed that for the first time, reports of wind and air pressure from distant ports could reach a single office within hours.

[2] That office belonged to Robert FitzRoy, a naval officer who had went around the world as captain of HMS Beagle, the ship that carried the young Charles Darwin. In 1854 FitzRoy became head of a new government department. Its job was to collect weather data for sailors. A storm in 1859 that sank the passenger ship Royal Charter persuaded him of one thing, the data could be used to warn of storms before they arrived. By 1861 his office was sending storm warnings by telegraph to ports, where signals were hoisted for ships in harbor to see.

[3] Later that year FitzRoy went further. [A] Beginning in August 1861, The Times of London printed his forecasts for the general public. [B] Each forecast gave the expected wind and weather for several regions of Britain over the following two days. [C] FitzRoy himself chose the word forecast for these notices, explaining that they were informed judgments rather than prophecies. [D]

[4] The forecasts were often wrong, and the number of letters complaining about the errors was growing. Some scientists argued that the forecasts had no sound theory behind it and that a government office should not publish guesses. FitzRoy, who had defended the work in print, was by then in failing health, and he died in 1865. The next year, after a review judged his methods unreliable, the public forecasts were stopped.

[5] Therefore, the storm warnings were back within two years, restored after complaints from ports and fishing towns, and daily forecasts returned to the newspapers more than a decade later. Today's forecasts rest on satellites and computer models that FitzRoy could not have imagined, but they still begin where his did, with many observations gathered quickly in one place.
prompt: In paragraph 4, in the sentence "FitzRoy, who had defended the work in print, was by then in failing health, and he died in 1865," which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "FitzRoy, who had defended the work in print, was"?
choices: No Change
FitzRoy who had defended the work in print, was
FitzRoy, who had defended the work in print was
FitzRoy who had defended the work in print was
explanation: A proper name already identifies the person, so a clause that follows it, here "who had defended the work in print," is nonessential and is set off by a pair of commas. Leaving out the first comma puts a lone comma between the subject phrase and its verb "was." Leaving out the second comma opens the clause without closing it. Leaving out both treats the clause as essential, as if it were needed to tell which FitzRoy is meant.

passage:
[1] When a news report announces that prices rose three percent last year, the figure almost always comes from a consumer price index. The idea behind such an index is simple enough to explain at a kitchen table. Picture a shopping basket that holds what a typical household buys in a month: bread, bus fares, rent, a haircut, a small share of a winter coat. Price the same basket a year later, and the change in its total cost shows how much more it takes to live the same way.

[2] Filling the basket is the hard part. In the United States, the Bureau of Labor Statistics decides what belongs in it by surveying thousands of households about what it spends. The weight given to each category depend on how much of the average budget it absorbs. Housing, which takes the largest share of most budgets, counts for far more than postage stamps. Each month, data collectors note the prices of tens of thousands of specific items at stores, clinics, and websites across dozens of cities. A collector who priced one brand of canned soup in March will look for the same can in April, the point is to compare like with like.

[3] The basket also has to keep up with the way people live. Some goods improve faster than their prices change. Statisticians therefore estimate how much of a price difference reflects better quality rather than inflation. Shoppers change, too. However, when the price of beef climbs, many shoppers buy more chicken, and an index that kept the old basket fixed would report a larger rise then the one most households actually felt.

[4] No real family buys exactly that basket. A renter who bikes to work and a homeowner with a long commute live through very different years, even when the headline number is the same for both. That is why economists treat the index as a careful average rather than a portrait of anyone's grocery bill, and why a particular household's prices can feel totally out of whack with the figure on the evening news.
prompt: In paragraph 2, in the sentence "A collector who priced one brand of canned soup in March will look for the same can in April, the point is to compare like with like," which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "April, the point is"?
choices: No Change
April, since the point is
April the point is
April; since the point is
explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone, which is a comma splice. Adding "since" makes the second clause subordinate and states the logical link: the collector looks for the same can because the point is to compare like with like. Removing the comma leaves a run-on with no connection at all. A semicolon must stand between two independent clauses, and "since the point is to compare like with like" is a dependent clause, so the semicolon is misused.

passage:
[1] Snow that falls on the high interior of Antarctica does not go anywhere. In places where summers never warm enough to melt it. Each winter's snow is buried by the next, and the weight of later layers slowly presses the older ones into solid ice. As the grains fuse, small pockets of air between them are sealed off.

[2] To reach that air, a drilling team bores down through the ice sheet and lifts out a core: a cylinder of ice about as wide as a coffee can, brought up in sections a few meters long. Stored at temperatures far below freezing, scientists can keep the cores for decades. Back in the laboratory, researchers crush small pieces of ice in a vacuum and look at the gases that escape. The deepest cores from Antarctica reaches back roughly 800,000 years, and the cores' oldest layers hold air that has been sealed away ever since.

[3] What that air shows is striking. During the coldest stretches of the ice ages, carbon dioxide stood at around 180 parts per million; in the warm periods between them, it rose to roughly 280. The ice carries a second record as well. The ratio of heavy to light oxygen atoms in frozen water depends on how cold the air was when the snow formed. Nonetheless, each layer tells researchers how cold it was as well as what the air held. When scientists first lined up the two records in the late 1980s, they find that carbon dioxide and temperature had risen and fallen together.

[4] Today the level is above 400 parts per million, higher than at any point in the ice's record. Against a history measured in hundreds of thousands of years, the speed of the recent change is what stands out most. The cores cannot say what comes next, but they can show what the planet was like each time its air changed before.
prompt: In paragraph 1, in the sentences "In places where summers never warm enough to melt it. Each winter's snow is buried by the next, and the weight of later layers slowly presses the older ones into solid ice," which choice makes the writing most grammatically acceptable in place of "it. Each winter's snow"?
choices: No Change
it, each winter's snow
it; each winter's snow
it, and each winter's snow
explanation: "In places where summers never warm enough to melt it" is a dependent clause and cannot stand alone as a sentence, so as written it is a fragment. Attaching it with a comma to the independent clause that follows, "each winter's snow is buried by the next," makes it an introductory element. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, so it cannot follow the dependent clause. Adding "and" joins the dependent clause to the main clauses as though they were equals, which leaves the whole sentence without a main clause to attach to.

passage:
[1] At sixty-eight, I assumed I knew how to grow a tomato. I had, after all, eaten thousands of them. So when a plot opened up in the community garden behind the public library last spring, I signed the waiver, paid my forty dollars, and accepted a key to a padlock that, I would discover, opened only on the third try.

[2] My plot, number fourteen, sat between two experts. On one side was Marguerite, a retired chemistry teacher who labeled her rows with laminated cards. On the other was a young couple whose beans climbed a trellis. They had built the trellis from salvaged bicycle wheels. I had a trowel, a borrowed hose, and a great deal of optimism. Marguerite and I soon reached an understanding, she would give advice, and I would ignore it.

[3] I planted in April, which Marguerite said was too early, and again in May, which she said was too late. That first month I learned to water in the morning, to thin my seedlings, and that slugs come out at night. Marguerite's tomatoes stood in tidy cages by the end of June. Similarly, mine sprawled across the path, where the young couple stepped over them each evening with exaggerated care.

[4] The garden's coordinator, a patient man named Desmond posted a sign in July asking members to check their squash plants for vine borers. I read the sign, admired the lettering, and went home to lunch. By the time I noticed the borers in my own plot, they already ate through three stems.

[5] My harvest, when it came, was modest: eleven tomatoes, a colander of beans, and one zucchini I had overlooked until it reached the size of my forearm. I have renewed the plot for next year. Marguerite has already offered her advice, and I have decided, for once, to take some of it.
prompt: This question asks about the preceding passage as a whole. Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to describe how a newcomer's confidence was tested by a first season of gardening. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?
choices: Yes, because it follows a narrator who thinks eating tomatoes is qualification enough through mistimed plantings, sprawling vines, and lost squash.

explanation: The essay opens with the narrator assuming that having "eaten thousands" of tomatoes means knowing how to grow one, then follows the plantings Marguerite calls too early and too late, the sprawling tomatoes, and the squash lost to borers, and ends with the narrator ready to take advice. That is confidence tested. The neighbors' methods appear only as passing details, laminated cards and a bicycle-wheel trellis, not as described methods. The narrator does not end as sure as at the start, since the last sentence has the narrator deciding to take some of Marguerite's advice. And Marguerite is absent from paragraphs 1 and 4; the essay is about the narrator.
